section.title: Justified by Faith, Not Works
section.sectionRationale: Here the letter reaches its theological heart. Paul recounts confronting Peter at Antioch for withdrawing from Gentile believers, and turns the incident into the clearest statement of the gospel: a person is not justified by works of the law but by faith in Jesus Christ. Paul has died to the law and been crucified with Christ, and he refuses to nullify the grace of God, for if righteousness came through the law, then Christ died for nothing.
section.thesis: No one is justified by works of the law but only by faith in Jesus Christ; the believer has been crucified with Christ so that Christ now lives in him, and to seek righteousness through the law is to set aside the grace of God and make Christ's death pointless.
section.frameNote: Three movements: the confrontation at Antioch when Peter drew back from Gentiles; the great thesis that justification is by faith in Christ, not works of the law; and the crucified life, I have been crucified with Christ, and the refusal to nullify grace.

units.label: Confronting Peter at Antioch
units.note: not walking in line with the truth of the gospel

verses.text: When Cephas came to Antioch, however, I opposed him to his face, because he stood condemned.
For before certain men came from James, he used to eat with the Gentiles. But when they arrived, he began to draw back and separate himself, for fear of those in the circumcision group.
The other Jews joined him in his hypocrisy, so that by their hypocrisy even Barnabas was led astray.

When I saw that they were not walking in line with the truth of the gospel, I said to Cephas in front of them all, “If you, who are a Jew, live like a Gentile and not like a Jew, how can you compel the Gentiles to live like Jews?”

units.label: Not by works of the law but by faith
units.note: the great thesis of the letter

verses.text: We who are Jews by birth and not Gentile “sinners”

know that a man is not {{dikaioo|justified}} by works of the {{nomos|law}}, but by {{pistis|faith}} in Jesus Christ. So we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, because by works of the law no one will be justified.

units.label: Crucified with Christ
units.note: I no longer live, but Christ lives in me

verses.text: But if, while we seek to be justified in Christ, we ourselves are found to be sinners, does that make Christ a minister of sin? Certainly not!
If I rebuild what I have already torn down, I prove myself to be a lawbreaker.
For through the law I died to the law so that I might live to God.
I have been {{systauroo|crucified with Christ}}, and I no longer live, but Christ lives in me. The life I live in the body, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me and gave Himself up for me.
I do not set aside the grace of God. For if righteousness comes through the law, then Christ died for nothing.

dikaioo.gloss: To justify, to declare righteous, to acquit. This is a courtroom word: God the judge pronounces the guilty sinner righteous in His sight. Paul insists this verdict comes not by works of the law but by faith in Christ. Justification is not being made gradually better; it is being declared right with God on the basis of Christ's finished work.

nomos.gloss: Law, especially the law of Moses with its commands. Works of the law are the deeds the law requires, including its badges of covenant membership like circumcision. Paul's point is that no amount of law keeping can justify a sinner, because the law can command righteousness but cannot supply it. The law was never given to be the way of acceptance with God.

pistis.gloss: Faith, trust, reliance. Justifying faith is not a work we perform to earn favor but the empty hand that receives what Christ has done. Paul contrasts faith in Jesus Christ with works of the law as two utterly different grounds of acceptance. Faith looks away from self to the Son of God who loved me and gave Himself for me.

systauroo.gloss: To crucify together with. Paul says he has been crucified with Christ: in union with Him, his old self under the law's condemnation has died, and the risen Christ now lives in him. This is the deep logic of the gospel, that the believer is so joined to Christ that His death and life become the believer's own.

basic.context: Paul tells of the day he had to correct Peter himself. At Antioch Peter had freely eaten with Gentile believers, but when strict Jewish visitors arrived, he drew back and separated himself, and others followed, even Barnabas. Paul saw this as a betrayal of the gospel and confronted Peter publicly. Then he states the heart of the whole letter: no one is justified by works of the law, only by faith in Christ.
basic.hermeneutics: The Antioch story is not gossip; it sets up the doctrine. Peter's behavior implied that Gentiles were second class until they kept Jewish law, which denies that faith in Christ is enough. Paul's response gives us the classic definition of justification. Read verses 15 to 21 as the theological center of Galatians.
basic.originalLanguages: The key word is dikaioo, to justify, to be declared righteous by God the judge. It comes not by works of the nomos, the law, but by pistis, faith, in Jesus Christ. And Paul describes union with Christ by systauroo, crucified together with Him, so that Christ now lives in him.
basic.typology: The law that pronounced a curse on lawbreakers is answered by Christ who bore that curse. Dying to the law so as to live to God fulfills the pattern of death and resurrection: the old life under condemnation ends, and new life in Christ begins, which the sacrifices and the exodus only pictured.
basic.christ: Christ is everything here. He is the object of justifying faith, the one who loved me and gave Himself up for me, and the one whose death is emptied of meaning if righteousness could come by law. The believer is crucified with Him and now lives by Him. If we could be saved by works, then Christ died for nothing.
basic.god: God is the judge who justifies, declaring sinners righteous on the basis of Christ, not works. He is the God whose grace Paul refuses to set aside. The whole passage guards the freeness of God's grace: to add works is to insult the God who gave His Son so that we might be accepted for Christ's sake alone.
basic.crossReferences: Romans 3 says all are justified freely by grace through faith in Christ. Romans 6 speaks of being united with Christ in His death and raised to new life. Ephesians 2 says we are saved by grace through faith, not by works.
basic.oneStory: The whole Bible asks how a sinner can stand before a holy God. Here is the answer at its clearest: not by our works but by faith in Christ, who was crucified in our place. The believer, crucified with Christ, now lives a new life by faith in the Son of God who loved him.

context.literary:
The passage has the shape of a funnel. It begins with a narrated event at Antioch, verses 11 to 14, moves into a statement of shared Jewish conviction in verses 15 and 16, and narrows to the first person singular in verses 19 and 20, where Paul stops reporting what he said to Peter and simply confesses what has happened to him. Where the speech to Peter ends and Paul's own address to the Galatians begins is not marked in the Greek. The BSB footnote notes that some translators close the quotation after verse 16 or verse 21. That blur may be deliberate, since what Paul said to Peter is exactly what he now says to his readers.

The key terms repeat in a tight pattern. The verb 'justify' and the phrase 'works of the law' occur three times each in verse 16, set against 'faith in Christ' twice, so that the verse reads like a legal sentence being hammered into the memory. The sentence ends with a quiet allusion to Psalm 143:2, where no living person is righteous before God, and Paul adds the word 'law' to sharpen it. Verses 17 and 18 are an objection and a reply, a style Paul often borrows from the street debate, closed by his usual 'Certainly not!' Verse 21 is the final balance, with one side 'the grace of God' and the other 'Christ died for nothing.'

The passage also sits at a hinge in the whole letter. Chapters 1 and 2 are Paul's autobiography, offered as evidence that his gospel came from Christ and was recognised by the pillars at Jerusalem. The Antioch scene is the last chapter of that evidence, and it carries the story from a private agreement in Jerusalem to a public test of whether the agreement would be lived. Chapters 3 and 4 then turn to argument from experience and Scripture. Verse 16 is therefore the first full statement of the thesis that the rest of the letter defends.
context.historical:
Antioch on the Orontes was the third city of the empire and the place where believers were first called Christians, Acts 11:26. Its church was mixed from the start, Jews and Gentiles sharing meals, and it was the base from which Paul and Barnabas were sent out, Acts 13:1-3. Eating together was the daily proof of the gospel's reach. For devout Jews, shared tables with Gentiles raised questions of food laws and ritual purity, and Peter had already crossed that line when God sent him to the household of Cornelius, Acts 10:28 and 11:3.

Who 'certain men from James' were, and what authority they carried, is only partly clear. The text says they came 'from James,' not that James sent them with this message, and Paul's phrase 'the circumcision group' names the pressure Peter feared rather than the men's official standing. In the years when Judea was uneasy, any Jewish believer seen eating freely with Gentiles may have invited trouble from zealous neighbours, so fear could have been mixed with prudence. Paul calls it what it was in effect, a retreat that made Gentile believers second class.

The date of the scene is debated. Many place it after the Jerusalem agreement of Galatians 2:1-10, others put the Jerusalem visit of this chapter at the famine visit of Acts 11 and treat the Antioch incident as earlier or around the time of Acts 15. Paul's argument does not depend on the answer. Barnabas, who had been Paul's partner, is drawn into the withdrawal, which shows how heavy the pressure was and why Paul's public rebuke cost him personally. Paul's firmness here is the same firmness he showed with Titus in Galatians 2:3-5, where he refused to let a Gentile believer be forced into circumcision.
context.canonical:
The passage rests on the great Old Testament theme of the separation of clean from unclean, and it announces the end of that separation as a barrier among God's people. Leviticus 20:24-26 grounds the food laws in Israel's being set apart from the nations. Peter's rooftop vision, Acts 10:9-16, and the Jerusalem council of Acts 15 were the earlier steps by which the church learned that the wall no longer stood. Galatians 2:11-14 shows how hard it was to live that out, even for an apostle who had seen the vision.

The confession of verses 15 and 16 stands inside a chain of New Testament statements of the same truth. Romans 3:20-28 repeats the language of justification apart from works of the law almost word for word. Philippians 3:9 gives Paul's own testimony of wanting a righteousness that comes through faith in Christ, not from the law. Ephesians 2:8-9 says the same of salvation as a whole, and Titus 3:5-7 anchors it in mercy and rebirth. Behind all of these lies Psalm 143:2, whose line about no one living being righteous before God Paul takes as the settled verdict of Scripture.

The 'crucified with Christ' of verse 20 links forward to Romans 6:1-14, where the same union with His death is spelled out as the believer's break with sin, and to Romans 7:1-6, where it is the believer's release from the law as a ruling authority. It also anticipates Galatians 5:24 and 6:14, where Paul speaks of the flesh and the world as crucified. The final sentence, that Christ would have died for nothing, is the negative side of the claim made in 1 Corinthians 15:3 that He died for our sins.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
Paul wants the Galatians to see that the issue at stake in their churches is the very one he faced at Antioch. The question is not whether Jewish believers may keep their customs, but whether anyone should be made to believe that fellowship with God or with God's people depends on them. By telling the story of Peter, Paul takes the heat out of a personal fight and puts it into a principle: if even Peter's behaviour could contradict the gospel, then the Galatians' flirtation with the law is not a small thing either.

Verses 15 and 16 are designed as common ground. Paul says 'we' who are Jews by birth know this, which puts him and Peter, and by implication the Jewish teachers who unsettled Galatia, on the same side of the premise. If Jewish believers themselves put their trust in Christ because the law could not justify, how can they ask Gentiles to go the other way? The charge of verse 14 is therefore not hypocrisy about eating but hypocrisy about faith: acting as if Christ were not enough.

Verses 19 and 20 are his reply to the fear that grace makes people careless. Paul does not say that believers are excused from living well. He says the old self, under the law's sentence, has died, and a new life now runs on Christ's life within. The first hearers were meant to feel both the freedom and the cost: nothing left to earn, and nothing left to hold back.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The Antioch story is a record of what happened, not a command to publicly rebuke every leader who falters. Paul does not tell the Galatians to confront their elders in the street; he tells them what the cost of acting against the gospel is, and what it looks like when someone refuses to nullify grace. What is prescriptive is the principle, which Paul states plainly in verses 16 and 21 and which the rest of the New Testament repeats.

Some details are descriptive only. Peter's withdrawal and Barnabas's being led astray are cautions, not norms. Paul's public confrontation is recorded as the right response in that setting, because the offence was public and the gospel was at risk, but Matthew 18:15-17 and Galatians 6:1 show that private and gentle correction is the ordinary pattern. The passage does not claim that conflict is to be sought.

The claim about being crucified with Christ is a statement about every believer and not a special experience of Paul's. Romans 6 says the same of all who were baptised into Christ. For readers today it means that the question to ask when we are tempted to rest on our performance, or on someone else's, is whether we are acting as people who have died to that way of standing before God. It does not mean we have no part in obeying; Galatians 5:6 says faith works through love.

debates.question: Does 'faith in Jesus Christ' in verse 16 mean our faith, or the faithfulness of Christ?

views.label: Our faith in Christ
views.case: The Greek phrase pistis Christou can be read as a genitive of the object, so that the faith is directed at Christ. The sentence goes on to say 'we, too, have believed in Christ Jesus, that we may be justified by faith in Christ,' which makes the believer's act of trust explicit. Most English translations, including the BSB, and the Reformation tradition read it this way.

views.label: The faithfulness of Christ
views.case: Others read the genitive as subjective, so Paul speaks of Christ's own faithful obedience, unto death, as the ground of justification, with human believing named separately. They point to the pattern in Romans 3:22 and 3:26 and to the way verse 20 describes Christ as the one who 'loved me and gave Himself up for me.' The phrase 'by faith in Jesus Christ' then becomes 'through the faithfulness of Jesus Christ.'

debates.bearing: Both readings agree that justification rests on Christ and not on our law-keeping, and verse 16 itself names human believing in the very next clause. Whichever reading is chosen, the gospel is that we receive what He did, rather than add to it.

debates.question: What does Paul mean by 'works of the law'?

views.label: Law-keeping in general as a way to earn standing
views.case: On the traditional reading the phrase means obedience to the Mosaic law offered as a ground of acceptance. Verse 16 ends with 'by works of the law no one will be justified,' and the quotation in 3:10-12 shows Paul has all the law's demands in view, with the curse falling on those who do not 'continue to do everything written.'

views.label: Law-keeping that marks off Israel from the nations
views.case: Others stress that the immediate setting is circumcision, food laws and table fellowship, the practices that separated Jew from Gentile. On this view Paul's target is the use of those boundary markers as the sign of belonging to God's people, though most who hold it grant that Paul's argument reaches to law-keeping in general.

debates.bearing: The Antioch scene supports the second emphasis and Galatians 3:10-12 supports the first. The two are not rivals: asking Gentiles to keep Jewish customs as the price of acceptance is a form of trying to be right with God by law.

debates.question: When did the Antioch confrontation take place?

views.label: After the Jerusalem agreement
views.case: Reading the letter in order, Paul describes the Jerusalem meeting of 2:1-10 and then Antioch. Peter's behaviour would then be all the more shocking, since he had just agreed that Gentiles need not be circumcised. Many place both after the council of Acts 15.

views.label: Before the council, or around it
views.case: Others hold that the Jerusalem meeting of Galatians 2 is the earlier famine visit of Acts 11 and that the Antioch trouble helped provoke the council of Acts 15. On this view the incident explains why the council was needed, and Acts 15:1-2 describes the same controversy from Luke's side.

debates.bearing: The timing changes the colour of Peter's lapse but not Paul's point. In either case the gospel of grace is shown to be what keeps the church together.

study.originalLanguages:
The verb that Paul uses of Peter in verse 12, 'draw back,' is hypostello, a word that means to shrink or withdraw, as a soldier pulls back from the front. It is the same verb the Greek Bible uses in Habakkuk 2:4 and that Hebrews 10:38 repeats: 'if he shrinks back, My soul will have no pleasure in him.' Paul is not describing a change of mind but a retreat under fear, and the same verse of Habakkuk gives him the text, 'The righteous will live by faith,' that he will quote in 3:11. Peter's shrinking back is the opposite of living by faith. The companion verb, aphorizo, 'separate himself,' is a verb of setting apart, the very word Paul uses in 1:15 of God who 'set me apart from my mother's womb.' God set Paul apart for the gospel; fear set Peter apart from his brothers.

The hypocrisy of verse 13 is hypokrisis, a stage word that first meant acting a part on a stage. The verb synypokrinomai, 'joined him in hypocrisy,' is the same idea with the prefix of company, so that Jewish believers and Barnabas were acting a role together. It is not that Peter did not believe in the gospel; it is that his conduct played a different script.

When Paul says in verse 14 that they were 'not walking in line with' the gospel, he uses a verb built from 'straight' and 'foot,' a picture of walking a straight course. The standard is not a rule but the truth of the gospel itself. The charge that follows uses ioudaizo, 'live like Jews,' a word that speaks of a way of life, not a creed, and anankazo, 'compel,' the same verb used of the pressure to circumcise Titus in 2:3 and of the troublemakers in 6:12. Peter's example was working as pressure even though he spoke no word.

In verse 18, 'tear down' is katalyo, a builder's word, and 'rebuild' is oikodomeo. The wall that Paul tore down was the old dependence on the law as the way to stand before God. To rebuild it is to confirm that the law was right to condemn, and so 'prove myself to be a lawbreaker,' parabates, a word for one who steps across a line. And in verse 20, 'crucified with' is in the perfect tense, which means a completed act whose results continue: Paul was crucified with Christ, and remains so. Then 'I live' is present, so the life he now lives is the continuous result of that death.

typology.type: The separation of clean from unclean, Leviticus 20:24-26
typology.fulfillment: Israel was set apart from the nations by laws of food and purity, and the table at Antioch shows how deeply those laws shaped daily life. Peter's retreat exposes the way a type can be mistaken for the reality. In Christ the dividing wall is taken down: Ephesians 2:14-16 says He made the two groups one and reconciled both in one body through the cross. The sign of separation has given way to the thing it pointed to, a holy people drawn from every nation. The type falls short because the laws set apart a nation; Christ sets apart a people from every tongue, without boundary of ancestry.

typology.type: The torn down and rebuilt wall, Galatians 2:18
typology.fulfillment: Paul speaks as if the law had been a building he took apart, and to put it back would be to say that the demolition was a mistake. The same pattern runs through the Old Testament temple, which stood as the place where heaven and earth met until Christ's death tore the veil, Matthew 27:51. Hebrews 10:19-20 says the way into God's presence now stands open through His flesh. To rebuild the old barrier is to close a door that Christ opened. The type breaks down here in that the temple's walls were holy; Paul does not say the law was bad, only that it cannot be rebuilt as the way in.

Israel passed from slavery to freedom through water and death in the exodus, and the believer's life follows a similar shape, dying with Christ and rising to a new life. Romans 6:3-6 describes baptism as joining the believer to His death, and Colossians 3:3 says that the believer's life is now hidden with Christ in God. In Christ the pattern becomes personal, no longer a national event but a union with a person. The type falls short in that the exodus freed a people from an earthly master, whereas Christ frees a person from the reign of sin and the law's curse.

typology.type: The one who gave Himself up, Galatians 2:20
typology.fulfillment: The Servant of Isaiah 53:12 pours out His life unto death and bears the sin of many, and Paul sees this fulfilled in the Son who 'loved me and gave Himself up for me.' Ephesians 5:2 says the same of Christ's love, calling it a fragrant offering and sacrifice to God. The correspondence is that of love, shown in giving. What is new in Christ is the 'me': Paul does not say Christ died for humanity in general only, but for him by name. The type is outdone because no Old Testament sacrifice could say 'for me' with such personal certainty.

study.christ:
The passage moves toward Christ by three paths. First, He is the ground of justification. Verse 16 does not say that we are justified by faith as such, as if faith were a work that earns a reward, but by faith in Christ, so that the weight rests on the one in whom we trust. Paul's second 'in Christ' in verse 17 completes the thought: believers seek to be justified in Him, in union and not at a distance. Whatever the sense of the phrase 'faith in Jesus Christ,' every reading of it places Christ at the centre of the verdict.

Second, He is the life inside the believer. 'Christ lives in me' is not a figure of speech for good influence. In the Greek the believer's old existence has ended in the crucifixion of Christ, and the life he now lives is Christ's own risen life carried in a body of flesh. That is why Paul can say that the life 'in the body' is lived 'by faith in the Son of God.' The title 'Son of God' in this verse is intimate. It is the Son who loved and gave Himself, and the phrase 'loved me' makes the cross a love story with a name attached. Romans 8:32 and Ephesians 5:2 say the same of the Father's and the Son's love.

Third, He is the reason the argument cannot be softened. Verse 21 closes the matter: if righteousness came through the law, Christ died for nothing. The Greek word for 'for nothing,' dorean, is the word John 15:25 uses of those who hated Jesus 'without cause.' To add works to Christ's death is not to complete it but to treat it as unnecessary. The cross is the dividing line, and every attempt at self-righteousness, whether Jewish or Gentile, is judged by it.

There is a further link to the whole letter. The Christ who died is the Christ who 'gave Himself up for our sins to rescue us from this present evil age,' 1:4, and the one 'portrayed as crucified' before the Galatians' eyes in 3:1. The Antioch confrontation, the great thesis, and the crucified life all point at one event. For readers, the guard against forced allegory is to remember that Paul does not use Peter as a type of anything; the lesson is plain and comes from what Paul says, that nothing may stand beside Christ in the way we are accepted by God.
study.god:
The God of this passage is first of all the judge who declares a verdict. The verb 'justify' belongs to the courtroom, and in verse 16 God is the unnamed subject of the passive 'is justified,' so the one who acquits is the one who is offended. That tells us something about holiness: the verdict is not a pretence, and Psalm 143:2, which Paul echoes, says that no living person can stand before God on their own record. At the same time God is the one who gives the verdict in our favour. The tension between His justice and His mercy is not resolved by lowering His standards but by the cross, where the Son took the sentence.

He is also the God of grace in a sense Paul will not let anyone dilute. Verse 21 says that to seek righteousness through the law is to set aside the grace of God. Grace is not an extra on top of the law; it is the whole basis of the relationship. The Father who gave His Son is generous without being sentimental, and His gift cannot be improved upon by human additions. That has consequences for worship, since praise is the natural response to a verdict we did not earn.

The passage also shows God as one who unites. At Antioch the problem was a table divided by fear of what others would think, and the gospel claims that God is one God over Jew and Gentile alike, as Romans 3:29-30 says. A church that has two tiers of acceptance denies God's character as much as His word. The God who makes one family from many peoples does not tolerate a lesser fellowship.

Finally, the God of the passage is intimate. The Son is the one who loved and gave Himself, and the life that Paul lives is a life in union with Him. Verse 20 is not about a distant sovereign but about a presence within, and the same thought will return in 4:6, where the Spirit of the Son cries out in our hearts. For readers this reshapes the question of how to approach God: not with a ledger of obedience, but as those who have been crucified with the Son and are held by His love.

crossReferences.note: Peter's own confession that God had shown him not to call any person impure or unclean. This is what makes Galatians 2:12 so striking: Peter had already learned the lesson from heaven, and failed to hold it under social pressure.

At the Jerusalem council Peter speaks for grace, saying that Gentiles and Jews alike are saved through the grace of the Lord Jesus. If this scene comes first, Antioch is a lapse; if it comes after, Peter is recovering from it.

Earlier in the same chapter, Paul refused to let Titus be forced to circumcision. The pattern is the same as at Antioch: the freedom of the gospel is defended when pressure is brought to bear on a Gentile believer.

The verse behind the last clause of Galatians 2:16. The psalmist asks God not to bring His servant into judgment, because no one living is righteous in His sight. Paul reads that as the standing verdict of Scripture, which the law cannot overturn.

The fullest parallel to Galatians 2:16. Romans adds that God put Christ forward as a sacrifice of atonement and that justification is a gift. It also asks about boasting and answers that it is excluded.
The same union with Christ in His death that Paul states in Galatians 2:20, developed to answer the question whether grace allows sin. The reply is that believers have died to sin and live to God.
Paul's explanation of how a believer dies to the law, as a wife is freed from her husband's law by his death. It sheds light on 'through the law I died to the law' in Galatians 2:19.
Paul's testimony of counting his religious achievements as loss for the sake of Christ, wanting the righteousness that comes through faith in Christ and not his own from the law.
Paul's conviction that one died for all, therefore all died, and that those who live should no longer live for themselves. It is the same logic as being crucified with Christ and living by Him.

A summary of the doctrine in a few phrases: saved by grace through faith, not from works, so that no one may boast. It matches Galatians 2:16 and 2:21 and shows the teaching was the common faith of Paul's churches.

God saved us not because of righteous deeds we had done but according to His mercy, so that justified by grace we might become heirs. It joins justification to the Spirit's renewal and to inheritance, which Galatians will take up next.

The balancing statement for readers who fear that justification by faith makes obedience unimportant. In Christ neither circumcision nor uncircumcision counts for anything, only faith working through love. Faith that rests on Christ alone is never idle, because love is how it shows itself.

study.oneStory:
The question this passage answers is older than Israel. In Genesis 3 humanity hid from God behind leaves, trying to cover its own shame, and the rest of the Bible is the story of what God does about that. The law given at Sinai showed the problem more clearly without removing it, and Galatians 2:16 draws the conclusion that no one will be justified by it. Paul's insight is that the problem was never solved by trying harder. It could only be solved by someone else standing in the place of the guilty.

The scene at Antioch is the first great test of what that means in practice. For the Old Testament, Israel was one people among the nations, and the line between Israel and the rest was real and God-given. When the Messiah came, the line that had carried the promise began to open, so that the nations could come in, as the prophets had said. Peter's retreat showed that the church was tempted to rebuild the line on the new ground, with the gospel as admission and the law as the actual membership test. Paul's rebuke was a defence of the very thing the prophets had promised, a people from every nation under one Lord.

What this passage sets up is chapters 3 and 4, where Paul will argue that Abraham himself was justified by faith, that the law came later, and that believers are sons and heirs. The crucified life of verse 20 is the first glimpse of the new creation: a person who has died to the old order and now lives from the risen Christ. Romans 8:1-4 and 2 Corinthians 5:17 describe the same reality as a new creation in which the old has passed away.

At the end of the story, Revelation 7:9 shows a great multitude from every nation, tribe, people and language standing before the throne. No one there carries a ledger of works. They are there on the strength of the Lamb, as Paul says of himself here, because the Son of God loved them and gave Himself for them. Every table at Antioch that ever stood divided will be gathered into that one feast.

sermon.title: Justification by Faith Alone (Galatians 2:11 to 21)
sermon.why: Begg expounds Paul's confrontation with Peter and the great thesis that a person is justified by faith in Christ and not by works of the law, drawing out the meaning of being crucified with Christ and living by faith in the Son of God.

quiz.q: Why did Paul confront Peter at Antioch?

options.text: Because his withdrawal from Gentile believers denied the truth of the gospel.
options.note: Peter's separation implied Gentiles were second class without the law.

options.text: Because Peter had preached a false sermon.
options.note: The issue was Peter's conduct at the table, not a sermon.

options.text: Because of a personal grudge between them.
options.note: Paul acted to defend the gospel, not out of personal offense.

options.text: Because Peter had denied being an apostle.
options.note: Peter's apostleship was not in question; his hypocrisy was.

quiz.q: How is a person justified, according to verse 16?

options.text: By faith in Jesus Christ, not by works of the law.
options.note: The verse states the thesis three times over.

options.text: By a combination of faith and law keeping.
options.note: Paul excludes works of the law entirely as a ground of justification.

options.text: By sincere effort to obey the commandments.
options.note: By works of the law no one will be justified.

options.text: By being born into the right family.
options.note: Even Jews by birth are justified only by faith in Christ.

quiz.q: What does Paul mean by I have been crucified with Christ?

options.text: In union with Christ his old self has died, and Christ now lives in him.
options.note: Verse 20 describes union with Christ in His death and life.

options.text: That he must earn salvation by suffering like Christ.
options.note: It is union with Christ's death, not a way to earn salvation.

options.text: That he no longer has any real personal existence.
options.note: He still lives in the body, but now by faith in the Son of God.

options.text: That the crucifixion was only symbolic.
options.note: The cross is utterly real; Paul is joined to the crucified Christ.

quiz.q: What would follow if righteousness could come through the law?

options.text: Then Christ died for nothing.
options.note: Verse 21 draws the stark conclusion of adding law to grace.

options.text: Then the law would need to be kept more strictly.
options.note: The point is not stricter law but that Christ's death would be pointless.

options.text: Then faith would still be the main thing.
options.note: If law could justify, faith in Christ would be unnecessary, not merely secondary.

options.text: Then God's grace would be even greater.
options.note: It would empty grace, not magnify it.

quiz.q: How does Paul describe Christ's love in verse 20?

options.text: The Son of God who loved me and gave Himself up for me.
options.note: The atonement is made deeply personal.

options.text: A distant love shown only to the whole world in general.
options.note: Paul makes it personal, loved me and gave Himself for me.

options.text: A love that depends on how well Paul performs.
options.note: The love is grounded in Christ's self giving, not Paul's performance.

options.text: A love shown only to the apostles.
options.note: It is the love every believer receives in Christ.

questions: Peter's fear of others led him to act against the gospel he believed. Where does fear of what people think tempt you to live inconsistently with the gospel?
Justification means God declares you righteous by faith in Christ, not by your performance. How would resting in that verdict change the way you face your failures?
Paul says Christ lives in me and I live by faith in the Son of God. What does it look like, practically, to live each day by faith in Christ rather than by self effort?
To add works to grace is to say Christ died for nothing. What are you tempted to add to Christ as if His finished work were not enough?
Christ loved me and gave Himself up for me. How does hearing the atonement in the first person, as personal love for you, move your heart today?

translationNotes.note: Faith in Jesus Christ renders a Greek phrase some translate as the faithfulness of Christ; the added clause so we too have believed in Christ Jesus supports the historic reading that it is the believer's faith directed to Christ.

The BSB footnote observes that some translators close Paul's quotation to Peter after verse 16 or 21; the doctrinal statement flows from the confrontation either way, and the point to Peter is the point to Galatia.
Crucified with Christ renders systauroo, crucified together with; it describes the believer's union with Christ in His death, not a call to earn salvation by suffering.

meta.notes: BSB text fetched from bible.helloao.org for Galatians 2:11-21. Sermon verified this session from the Truth For Life series A Study in Galatians, Volume 1 by Alistair Begg.
